name: Malta

income_tax.summary: Single resident rates for 2026: 0% to EUR 12,000, 15% to 16,000, 25% to 60,000 and 35% above. Employees pay 10% social security, self-employed 15%, both capped at about EUR 29,084 of annual income (maximum weekly contribution EUR 55.93 and EUR 83.89).
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed pay 15% of last year's net income, maximum EUR 83.89 a week for people born on or after 1 January 1962 (PwC). Cross-check: the employee fixed amount EUR 55.93 a week is 10% of a maximum weekly wage of EUR 559.30 (EUR 29,084 a year), and 15% of EUR 559.30 is EUR 83.90, so both maxima correspond to the same EUR 29,084 annual income; the recorded cap is therefore consistent, though PwC's wording is ambiguous. Part-time self-employment can qualify for 10% income tax capped at EUR 12,000.
income_tax.local_tax_note: No local income tax. The 0% band to EUR 12,000 stands in for the tax-free amount.

open_questions: PwC's wording ('EUR 55.93 per week for annual salaries exceeding EUR 29,084') is ambiguous; the arithmetic (10% x EUR 559.30 = 55.93; 15% x 559.30 = 83.90) supports reading it as the maximum contribution reached at EUR 29,084. The Maltese social security page returned 403.

Whether employee social security contributions are deductible from chargeable income could not be established from PwC (deductions and income determination pages are silent) or an official page (Commissioner for Revenue / CFR not reached); one secondary guide (Global Expansion) says they are not deducted, not relied on. Left null.

regimes.duration_note: Permit valid 1 year, renewable three times, 4 years in total (Residency Malta FAQ); renewal needs at least 5 of the previous 12 months in Malta. Tax: 0% in the first 12 months, 10% afterwards, so flat_rate 0.05 is the average over a 2-year stay (the persona horizon); over all 4 years the average would be 7.5%.
open_questions: Social security treatment of nomad permit holders is not stated in the Rules or on the Residency Malta pages (the FAQ says only that holders have no entitlement to a pension or social benefits); recorded as applying.

The 12-month exemption can be lost if the holder files a declaration that residence is not merely casual; a tax resident staying 2 years may need that declaration, in which case the first year is taxed at 10% too (not modelled; average would then be 10%).
The Residency Malta pages do not mention tax; the 10% and first-year rule come from S.L. 123.210.
regimes.name: Nomad Residence Permit
regimes.description: Permit for non-EU remote workers with minimum gross income of EUR 42,000 a year (about EUR 3,500 a month; EUR 32,400 for applicants before 1 April 2024), either employed by a foreign-registered employer, running a business for a foreign company they co-own, or freelancing for foreign clients with no fixed place of business in Malta. Tax (S.L. 123.210, L.N. 277/2023): the holder is chargeable at 10% on income from 'authorised work', defined as services provided REMOTELY for a non-resident employer or non-resident clients under a nomad residence permit that licenses work in Malta, so pay for work done while living in Malta is exactly the covered income (covers_local_work true). Rule 3(3): no tax on that income before the end of 12 months from permit issue (or 1 January 2024 if later) unless the holder declares his residence is not casual; the holder must still register for tax. Two-phase modelling: year 1 at 0% and year 2 onward at 10% gives an average of 5% over a 2-year stay, so flat_rate is 0.05 (7.5% over the full 4 years). Social security still treated as applying (not stated in the Rules).

open_questions: Whether self-employed individuals qualify is not covered; the sources mention employment income only.
Social security treatment is not covered; recorded as applying.
regimes.name: Highly Skilled Individuals Rules 2026 (15% rate)
regimes.description: Employment income from eligible offices (roles regulated or licensed by MFSA, MGA, Transport Malta, Malta Enterprise or the Chief Medical Officer) is taxed at 15% up to EUR 7,000,000 a year and at 35% above. Requires emoluments of at least EUR 65,000 a year (rising by EUR 10,000 every five years), relevant qualifications or five years of experience, non-domicile in Malta, suitable accommodation and medical insurance. Initial five years plus two five-year extensions; no benefit beyond 31 December 2040. In force from 1 January 2026, replacing the Highly Qualified Persons and sector rules.

costs.notes: The only figure with a stated method is island-wide; secondary guides (not opened) quote EUR 1,100 to 1,600 for a 1-bedroom in Sliema and St Julian's, so expat-area rents are probably well above these medians. A second rent source was not obtained: Global Property Guide returned 403 on re-check, Expatistan 403, Maltapark 404.

residence_routes: EU citizens can live and work freely with a registration. US and other non-EU remote workers use the Nomad Residence Permit (EUR 42,000 a year, one year renewable). Skilled non-EU employees get a single permit through a Maltese employer (Identità), which was not researched; the Highly Skilled Individuals Rules give the 15% rate for eligible roles for any nationality.
open_questions: Single-permit rules for skilled employees not researched.
The Sliema and St Julian's rent premium over the island-wide median is not quantified from an opened source.
Rents rest on one aggregator (island-wide medians); Sliema/St Julian's-specific rents not obtained from any opened source.
